Using the framework of cost modeling in DR-Path, we compute the annualized cost of enabling the response to dynamic pricing. The figures below summarize the median annualized 39 cost (in nominal USD) of new installations per site for each end use for the years 2019 and 2030. Figure 25. Annualized median cost of control technology to enable dynamic pricing response. The values shown in the figure considers only new installations in the residential sector. Figure 25 depicts the annualized cost (in nominal USD) of new installations of technologies that enable dynamic pricing response in the residential sector. As mentioned in Section 2.4, we use the cost assumptions from Phase 4 of California DR Potential Study for each representative DR enabling technology across end uses. A few observations are worth mentioning here. First, we can see that the annualized cost of end uses such as space cooling, heating, water heating, and Level 1 EV charging is relatively low. Additionally, even though a smart thermostat can be utilized for both space heating and space cooling end uses, we model their costs individually. This would imply that our estimation of cost-effective resources might be slightly conservative. Multifamily Level 2 EV charging is modeled as a shared resource utilized by multiple households; hence, it costs lower than Level 2 charging in single family houses. Next, the cost to enable pool pumps and spa pumps to respond to dynamic pricing is much higher compared to the other end uses. This is because there existed only one manufacturer of this control technology at the time of this data compilation in 2020. As a result of this lack of market maturity, the cost of these control technologies appears higher. With more manufacturers in the market, we expect these costs to reduce significantly in the future. 40 Figure 26. Annualized cost of control technology to enable dynamic pricing response. The values shown in the figure considers only new installations in the non-residential sector. Finally, Figure 26 shows the annual cost of new installations of technologies enabling dynamic price response in the non-residential sectors. Here, we see that the cost of installing technology to control agricultural pumping load is significantly higher than the other end uses because of the high initial costs of the technology. It is important to note that our cost assumptions for agricultural pumping does not include variable costs that scale with the site size (e.g., valves, sensors) due to the lack of data availability. 3.4.2 Cost benefit ratios Figure 27 shows the distribution of cost benefit ratio from responding to the dynamic pricing across all end uses for the 2030 low price forecast scenario. The distribution under a Full tariff is shown in green boxplots, followed by Medium in orange and Mild in blue. In general, we can see that the distribution of cost benefit ratios is smaller as the number of tariff components that are dynamic increases.
